A powered leg brace that helps people climb stairs again; security labels that cannot be copied; the weekly comparison.
TECH RADAR
A powered leg brace that gives back the stairs
No. 11 · Sunday 1 November 2026 · weekend overview · 6 min read
 
IN 30 SECONDS
1At the University of Utah, a motorised knee brace let three people with weak legs climb and descend stairs one foot after the other, something rigid braces do not allow.
2Korean and US researchers made security labels from liquid metal whose secret code appears only for a moment when heated, hidden among decoys.
3Weekly comparison: LLMs lead research, attacks on AI lead among developers, and energy is the only vertical slowing down.

new papers across the five verticals today

new LLM papers added to the archive today

robotics research momentum this year compared with all research
SIGNAL OF THE DAY
An active knee–ankle–foot brace that restores stair climbing
Advanced Intelligent Systems · 30 October · Free PDF  Journal  High-impact journal
Who wrote it: Brendon M. Ortolano and 4 others · University of Utah (United States) · among the authors Tommaso Lenzi, h-index 37
Context. People with very weak legs often wear a rigid brace from thigh to foot. It keeps the knee stable but cannot push, so walking is slow and unnatural, stairs are taken one step at a time, and over the years other joints suffer. Existing powered exoskeletons are either too weak or too stiff and slow.
The team built a brace with a compact motor at the knee, weighing 1.45 kg, that is both strong (up to 113 newton-metres of torque) and fast, yet easy to move freely when it is not pushing. Tests with one healthy volunteer showed it can deliver the same force and power as a human knee. In first clinical tests with three people with leg impairments, it let them climb and descend stairs step over step and walk better than with their usual passive brace. It is today's signal because it addresses a common, everyday disability with a device that works with the user's own movement rather than replacing it. The clinical test involved only three people.
PAPERS OF THE DAY · ONE PAPER PER VERTICAL
At the weekend, one paper for each vertical. Robotics is today's signal.
Aerospace · Space exploration and regulationgrowing
Research share +25% in 3 years · 1,562 papers in 2025
What it is about. Space is no longer just for governments: private companies launch rockets and satellites. Researchers increasingly study the rules, and the ideas, that come with this shift.
Visionaries Against Bureaucrats: How Space Entrepreneurs Remake Political Membership
Social Sciences · 30 October  Journal  Free PDF ↗
Who wrote it: Alin-Constantin Ionescu and 3 others · University of Bucharest, National University of Science and Technology Politehnica Bucharest (Romania), Technical University of Moldova (Moldova) · among the authors Daniel E. Rosner, h-index 48
WHAT THEY DOAn analysis of 31 public statements by Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos and Richard Branson from 2007 to 2026, about 128,500 words.
RESULTTheir talk draws a line between 'visionaries' and 'bureaucrats', presented as being about building rather than politics but landing on calls for deregulation, and it addresses a 'multiplanetary humanity' that has no vote while the infrastructure belongs to private companies.
WHY IT MATTERSA reminder that the space race also shapes ideas about who decides; one interpretive reading, by a single coder.
Energy · Battery materialsstable
Research share −4% in 3 years · 11,348 papers in 2025
What it is about. Sodium batteries use cheap, abundant sodium instead of lithium. Manganese-based materials store a lot of energy, but their structure warps during use and the battery wears out.
Alleviating the stability-energy density dilemma via electron-donor-mediated orbital symmetry regulation in sodium phosphate cathodes
Science Advances · 30 October  Journal  High-impact journal  Free PDF ↗
Who wrote it: Heng Zhang and 7 others · Northeast Normal University (China) · among the authors Xing-Long Wu, h-index 103
WHAT THEY DOAdding iron and vanadium to the manganese material spreads its electrons more evenly, which keeps its crystal from warping while preserving its energy.
RESULTThe material stores 492 Wh per kg and keeps 80.2% of its capacity after 2,000 cycles at a very fast charging rate.
WHY IT MATTERSIt eases the usual trade-off between energy and lifetime in sodium batteries, a cheaper option for grid storage.
LLMs · Language models and text analysisemerging
Research share +180% in 3 years · 11,876 papers in 2025
What it is about. Chatbots work best in English. How well do they handle smaller languages and specialised subjects?
Capabilities of Gemini, GPT, and DeepSeek for transportation in Dutch: Assessing domain-specific and underrepresented language challenges
European Journal of Transport and Infrastructure Research · 30 October  Journal  Free PDF ↗
Who wrote it: Thi M. D. Tran and 7 others · Hasselt University (Belgium), University of Stirling (United Kingdom) · among the authors Geert Wets, h-index 62
WHAT THEY DONine models from the Gemini, GPT and DeepSeek families answer 972 questions on transport and traffic rules, in English and Dutch, some with images.
RESULTModels do better in English, but several handle Dutch well: DeepSeek R1 and GPT-4o perform well in both languages, while Gemini 1.5 Pro struggles with Dutch. All combine information from images and text well.
WHY IT MATTERSUseful for public bodies and companies choosing a model in a language other than English.
Cybersecurity · Hardware securitystable
Research share flat in 3 years · 684 papers in 2025
What it is about. To prove a product is genuine, it can carry a 'fingerprint' made of random physical features that cannot be manufactured twice. The risk is that someone records its responses and imitates them digitally.
Liquid-metal physical unclonable functions resistant to both physical and digital cloning
Nature Communications · 30 October  Journal  High-impact journal  Free PDF ↗
Who wrote it: Simok Lee and 11 others · Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, Kongju National University, Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (South Korea, United States) · among the authors Michael David Dickey, h-index 99
WHAT THEY DOLabels made from randomly mixed liquid-metal particles. At rest they reveal nothing; only during a short heating window does a unique heat pattern appear that can be turned into a code, while outside that window misleading patterns hide the real one. They also printed them as labels and QR codes.
WHY IT MATTERSAnti-counterfeiting that resists both copying the object and copying its data, useful for supply chains. The abstract gives no figures.

Same data as yesterday: research figures are refreshed tonight. Research: share of all papers compared with three years ago, and acceleration in 2026. Public funding: share of 2025 papers declaring public funding. GitHub: new projects, middle value of the vertical's searches, Q3 2026 vs Q3 2025.

In short: Looking back over the week: the verticals most tied to AI grow fastest in both research and code, while energy, aerospace and robotics grow more slowly but rely more on public money. Robotics is the one to watch: its research is accelerating this year more than in the previous three.
WORDS OF THE DAY
h-index — a measure of how often a researcher is cited: an h-index of 50 means 50 papers cited at least 50 times each. Above 40 usually indicates an established name in the field.
Orthosis — a brace worn on part of the body to support or correct it, such as a knee or ankle brace.
Physical unclonable function — a physical 'fingerprint' made of random features of a material, impossible to manufacture twice, used to prove an object is genuine.
Sodium-ion battery — a battery that uses sodium, found in ordinary salt, instead of lithium: cheaper, but so far it stores less energy.
WORTH WATCHING
Tomorrow the radar of the day is on aerospace, with research data refreshed tonight. Worth watching: larger clinical trials of powered braces like today's signal.
